title: Mapping data literacy trajectories in K–12 education
extended_summary:
This paper presents a systematic literature review of K–12 data literacy research rather than an intervention study. The authors ask how learning experiences across K–12 data literacy activities can be mapped using a common framework, especially as AI and machine learning increasingly require students to understand data-driven systems rather than only traditional rule-based programming. They propose a two-dimensional “data paradigms” framework based on logic (knowledge-based vs. data-driven) and explainability (transparent vs. opaque) and use it to characterize existing activities.

The review synthesizes 84 empirical studies published from 2019 to 2024 across computing education, mathematics education, STEM, and learning sciences contexts. The paper identifies four learning trajectories: keeping transparent, keeping data-driven, jumping, and bridging. Most activities remained within a single paradigm, especially data-driven/transparent or data-driven/opaque tasks, while comparatively few studies bridged multiple paradigms or moved learners gradually from rule-based to opaque ML systems.

The main conclusion is that K–12 data literacy instruction is fragmented and often lacks a shared vocabulary for describing progression across paradigms. The authors argue that making epistemic differences between rule-based and data-driven reasoning explicit could help educators design better learning progressions and scaffolds. Because this is a literature review and position paper, it does not provide direct comparative evidence on outcomes for reading or literacy instruction, nor does it evaluate generative AI tools in K–12 classrooms.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / machine learning conversational or data-driven systems used in K–12 learning; in this paper, the focus is on data literacy trajectories rather than a specific educational product.
identified_tools.use_case: Systematic literature review of K–12 data literacy interventions, including examples that involved AI/ML tools such as Teachable Machine, StoryQ, Zhorai, Machine Learning for Kids, and other ML-based learning environments.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper/systematic literature review that synthesizes prior K–12 data literacy studies but does not report a new empirical comparison of an AI tool against instruction or control conditions. It provides conceptual framing and categorization rather than causal evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: No direct outcome effects are reported for a tool in this paper, so there is no measurable instructional impact to rate. The paper does not provide effect sizes, comparative results, or student learning outcomes for reading or literacy.
